Orthopedics · published research

Knee osteoarthritis

PBM Database summary

Summary of the Evidence

Placebo-controlled reviews generally favor selected PBM protocols for knee pain. The estimated size varies between reviews, and certainty is mostly low or very low. Findings for disability and function are less consistent, especially when PBM is added to exercise.

Clinical trials have tested different wavelengths, doses, treatment schedules, and combinations with exercise. The results are therefore best read by outcome and protocol, rather than as one uniform effect.

Human and clinical evidence

The 2019 Stausholm meta-analysis included 22 placebo-controlled trials. It found lower pooled pain and disability with PBM than placebo after treatment and at follow-up. The pain estimates varied substantially between trials, and the larger dose-recommended subgroup estimates do not define a single protocol that will work across settings (Stausholm et al. 2019).

A 2024 placebo-controlled review included ten studies and 542 people. Its six-study analysis favored PBM for pain at rest, but the authors rated certainty very low and found no clear pooled effect on mobility. A separate 2024 wavelength network meta-analysis included 13 trials and 673 participants. It found lower pain versus sham, including favorable estimates for 904–905 nm and 785–850 nm, but no clear pooled improvement in function or stiffness. These wavelength estimates do not show that one band is directly superior to another (Oliveira et al. 2024; Fan et al. 2024).

A 2025 umbrella review rated knee-pain evidence low certainty and disability evidence moderate certainty. It reported a small standardized pain estimate alongside a larger disability estimate. The review methods and outcome groupings differ from the knee-specific meta-analyses, which helps explain why pooled conclusions are not identical (Son et al. 2025).

Individual sham-controlled trials also report pain benefits with particular regimens. A 47-person trial of 904 nm treatment favored PBM for pain and a knee-symptom score. A 2025 trial randomized 73 participants and analyzed 65, reporting lower pain with 790 nm treatment at nine sites than with sham or no-treatment comparisons (Fukuda et al. 2016; Maciel et al. 2025).

Trials that add PBM to exercise have mixed results. A 60-person trial found greater short-term pain reduction with a laser-and-LED cluster, but no clinically important between-group differences in function, strength, or balance. In a 62-woman study PBM reduced pain versus sham PBM but added no further gains in walking capacity or strength. A 127-person trial found no added benefit for pain, function, or quality of life when PBM was added to strengthening exercise (de Paula Gomes et al. 2018; Vassão et al. 2020; Jorge et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

Twenty-three animal studies use rat and rabbit models to examine pain-like behavior, joint inflammation, oxidative stress, and cartilage structure. In a rat model, 904 nm PBM at 18 J/cm² was associated with reduced pain responses, neutrophil activity, oxidative damage, and inflammatory cytokines (Yamada et al. 2020). Another rat study found improved weight support and mechanical allodynia, alongside changes in superficial cartilage, but no effect on overall locomotor activity (Balbinot et al. 2021).

Rabbit studies also report changes in cartilage and synovial tissue. Repeated 830 nm laser treatment was associated with reduced synovitis and cartilage damage in a progressive osteoarthritis model (Wang et al. 2014).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

An 808 nm cell-culture experiment found that chondrocyte proliferation changed with dose and measurement day. The same paper also reported cartilage and inflammatory-marker findings in a rat osteoarthritis model (Tim et al. 2022).

In a separate ex-vivo study, synovial membrane samples from six people with osteoarthritis were exposed to 807–811 nm light at 25 J/cm². The researchers reported altered expression of 11 proteins, including increased mitochondrial HSP60 in samples from three participants (Barabás et al. 2014).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical protocols span 808–1064 nm, with energy per point from 1.5 to 12.4 J, total energy from 7.5 to 3000 J, and energy density from 3.3 to 202.5 J/cm² in a 2024 placebo-controlled review. Treatments were delivered one to five times per week, with a median of ten sessions and five to fifteen treatment points around the knee. The broad ranges reflect differences in devices, output, treatment area, and study design (Oliveira et al. 2024).

The older Stausholm review described dose-recommended ranges of 4–8 J per point for 785–860 nm and 1–3 J per point for 904 nm. Individual examples include 904 nm at 3 J per point over nine points, 790 nm at 4 J per point over nine sites, and a pulsed 905 nm laser combined with 875 nm and 640 nm LEDs. These schedules differ in session frequency, treatment sites, and use alongside exercise (Stausholm et al. 2019; Fukuda et al. 2016; Maciel et al. 2025; de Paula Gomes et al. 2018).

Trials also vary in application location, comparator, exercise co-treatment, and follow-up. Some test PBM alone against sham, while others add it to exercise or rehabilitation. A result for one combination or schedule should not be read as a result for every knee PBM protocol.

Interpretation

Selected PBM protocols have reduced knee pain compared with sham, and some reviews report meaningful pain or disability effects. Confidence in the size of those effects remains limited because reviews reach different estimates and treatment protocols vary widely. Disability and function are less settled, particularly when PBM is added to exercise. The findings are best interpreted by outcome, comparator, and regimen.

Publications and records 62 database records
Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Pain, Stausholm et al. 2019. Compared with placebo, the mean difference was 14.2 mm on a 100-mm scale after treatment (95% CI 7.3–21.1) and 15.9 mm at follow-up (6.5–25.4). Dose-recommended subgroup estimates were 18.7 mm (9.4–28.0) and 23.2 mm (10.6–35.9). The overall pain analyses were highly heterogeneous (I² = 93%) (Stausholm et al. 2019).

Disability, Stausholm et al. 2019. The pooled standardized mean difference was 0.59 after treatment (95% CI 0.33–0.86) and 0.66 at follow-up (0.23–1.09), favoring PBM. Dose-recommended subgroup estimates were 0.75 (0.46–1.03) and 1.31 (0.92–1.69) (Stausholm et al. 2019).

Pain at rest, Oliveira et al. 2024. Six studies gave a pooled SMD of −0.7 (95% CI −1.0 to −0.3), favoring PBM (Oliveira et al. 2024).

Pain versus sham, Fan et al. 2024. The pooled SMD was 0.96 (95% CI 0.31–1.61). Wavelength network estimates were 1.42 (0.31–2.53) for 904–905 nm and 0.82 (0.11–1.50) for 785–850 nm. These indirect estimates do not establish that one wavelength is superior (Fan et al. 2024).

Umbrella review, Son et al. 2025. Equivalent standardized mean differences (eSMDs) were 0.02 for pain (95% CI 0.01–0.03), rated low certainty, and 0.65 for disability (0.14–1.15), rated moderate certainty (Son et al. 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Pain: low certainty overall, with some reviews rating the pooled evidence very low. Results varied substantially between studies (Stausholm et al. 2019, Oliveira et al. 2024, Son et al. 2025).

Function and disability: findings vary by outcome. The 2025 umbrella review rated disability evidence moderate certainty, while a 2024 knee-specific review found no clear pooled benefit on a mobility measure. The findings suggest possible disability improvement, but not a consistent effect across functional measures (Oliveira et al. 2024, Son et al. 2025).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Pain results varied widely between studies. A 2024 review raised concerns about trial quality, and the 2025 umbrella review noted that smaller studies may influence its estimates. These issues limit confidence in one pooled estimate, though not necessarily equally for every treatment regimen (Stausholm et al. 2019, Oliveira et al. 2024, Son et al. 2025).

Reviews assessed different functional outcomes. The 2025 umbrella review rated disability evidence moderate, while a 2024 knee-specific review found no clear pooled benefit on a mobility measure. Findings are mixed by outcome, rather than one uniform effect (Oliveira et al. 2024, Son et al. 2025).
